title: OGLE-IV phases (2010-2024) show non-secular period changes in 43 of 105 blue large-amplitude pulsators; in the 55 secular ones, rates are small and 27 of 34 significant rates are positive
abstract: Question: Are the period changes of blue large-amplitude pulsators (BLAPs) secular, so that a measured rate r = (dP/dt)/P is an evolutionary rate? Pietrukowicz et al. (2025) found mostly positive rates near 1e-7 per year, which argues against contracting pre-white dwarfs, but they also reported irregular changes. Method: We measured seasonal pulsation phases of 166 OGLE BLAPs from OGLE-IV I-band data (2010-2024), OGLE-III/II data (1997-2009) for 29 stars, ZTF data (2018-2025) for 22 stars and Gaia DR3 epoch data for 23 stars. We tested quadratic (constant-rate) O-C models with a fitted phase jitter: full-record fits, rates from two independent halves of the record against a 2,000-run constant-rate Monte Carlo null, backward prediction of OGLE-III phases and forward prediction of 2018-2025 phases. Results: ZTF and Gaia phases agree with OGLE phases to 0.01-0.02 cycles, so the OGLE phases are reliable. With conservative error bars, a constant rate fails for a large part of the sample: the two-halves rate differences have a robust z scatter of 1.36 (null 0.97, p = 0.008) and 11% exceed 3 sigma (null 1.7%, p = 0.001). Rates fitted to 2010-2017 do not predict 2018-2025 phases better than a constant period (47 of 83 stars). A quadratic fitted to OGLE-IV predicts OGLE-III phases better than a linear ephemeris in 22 of 28 stars. We classify 55 of 105 stars as secular and 43 as non-secular (median phase jitter 0.077 cycles). Non-secular stars carry the large apparent rates (median 1.2e-6 per year) with no sign preference (10 of 17 positive). Secular stars have small rates (median 1.2e-7 per year) and 27 of 34 significant rates are positive (binomial p = 0.0008). Thus the positive-sign excess survives after removal of irregular stars, but rates of non-secular BLAPs are not evolutionary rates. Limitations: class boundaries depend on precision; season errors are about 1.5 times too small and we model this with jitter; ZTF adds little time span because bulge BLAPs are blended; we did not identify the cause of the irregular changes (binary light-travel time or stochastic period changes). display.caption: Seasonal O-C diagrams (cycles, relative to a linear ephemeris) of 12 BLAPs. Top row: secular class; the dashed line is the quadratic fit to OGLE-IV, extrapolated. Middle and bottom rows: non-secular class with turnovers, steps or failed backward extrapolation to OGLE-III/II. ZTF and Gaia DR3 phases are shown where available.

Two-halves test (conservative error model). Left: rates from the first and second half of each record. Right: distribution of z = (r2 - r1)/sigma against the constant-rate Monte Carlo null with white jitter.

Prediction tests. Left: OGLE-IV fits (2010-2024) predict OGLE-III/II phases; the quadratic ephemeris is better than the linear one. Right: fits to 2010-2017 predict 2018-2025; the quadratic is not better. Lines are running medians.

Pietrukowicz et al. 2025 (ApJS 279, 21): BLAP period change rates. We confirm the positive-sign excess in secular BLAPs and show that rates of irregular BLAPs depend on the time span; we use their published rates for comparison.
Pietrukowicz et al. 2017: definition of the BLAP class and the OGLE BLAP collection.
